666.title: Holding your hem
666.hook: leaving praise and blame, I have caught hold of Your hem, sung as the couple takes the scarf (Ramkali ki Var M5, ang 963)
666.howItsDone: At an Anand Karaj, while the bride's father places one end of the groom's palla in her hand, ragis sing Guru Arjan's line about letting go of praise and slander and holding the Lord's hem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, natural ease, and your line: round four: union. Today we step back to the moment just before the first round.

Before the four rounds begin, there's a small gesture that's easy to miss. The groom has a long scarf over his shoulder. The bride's father stands, takes one end of it, and places it in his daughter's hand. Nobody makes a speech. But the musicians are singing a line as it happens, and if you know the words, the gesture changes. Because the line isn't about the groom at all.
screen: `A SCARF OVER THE GROOM'S SHOULDER.` → `THE FATHER PLACES ONE END.` → `THE LINE BEING SUNG.`

segments.voice: The scarf is called the palla. The shabad sung as it's placed comes from Guru Arjan's Var in Raag Ramkali, on Ang nine sixty-three. In paraphrase: praise and slander, I have given them all up; I have let everything go. I have seen that all relationships are false, so I have caught hold of Your hem. It's startling to sing at a wedding. All relationships are false? On the day two families join? But the singer isn't the bride speaking to the groom. In Gurbani the soul is often the bride and God the Husband. The one whose hem she grabs is the Lord. So the shabad reminds everyone in the room of something tender and a little fierce: the deepest thing to hold on to, it says, isn't another person, even this beloved person. It's the One. One reading draws a lesson for the marriage too: two people who each hold God's hem aren't asking each other to be everything. Then look at what's let go first: praise and slander, ustat and nindaa. What people say about you, good or bad. A wedding is full of it: the clothes, the food, the gossip about the in-laws. The shabad drops all of it before the first step. The palla itself is just cloth. But held in a bride's hand, with that line in the air, it becomes a picture of a soul taking hold of what won't let go. The couple walks the four rounds holding it, so neither walks alone.
screen: `THE PALLA: THE WEDDING SCARF.` · `PRAISE AND SLANDER, LET GO.` · `THE HEM IS THE LORD'S.` · `TWO WHO EACH HOLD ON TO GOD.` · then, large: `HOLDING THE HEM.`

segments.voice: If someone you love is near, take their hand for a moment; if not, hold your own hands together, or something that belongs to someone you love, a scarf, a ring, a photo, and feel the simple fact of holding on. Then gently let go of one thing people say about you, good or bad, that you've been carrying. If you pray, say Waheguru as you hold.
Palla, the end of a scarf, a hem: Guru Arjan's line, sung as the bride takes it, lets go of praise and slander, as the soul catches hold of the Lord's hem.
Your line: holding the hem. Praise and slander can both be set down. See you tomorrow.

667.title: No hot wind touches
667.hook: no hot wind touches the one in the Lord's refuge (Bilaval M5, ang 819)
667.howItsDone: Sikhs often sing or recite taatee vaao na lagaee for protection and comfort: at a birth, before travel, in illness, or at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the palla, the hem the bride holds, and your line: holding the hem. Today, a shabad sung when someone loved needs protecting.

In a Punjabi June, the afternoon wind doesn't cool you. It burns. It comes off the plains like the air from an open oven, and people have a name for it: the loo. Shops pull their shutters, farmers rest under the trees, and mothers keep children indoors until evening. Where that wind blows, shade isn't a nice extra. It's survival. Guru Arjan turned that experience into a line of comfort.
screen: `A PUNJABI JUNE AFTERNOON.` → `THE WIND LIKE AN OVEN.` → `WHAT SHADE MEANS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang eight nineteen, and it opens: taatee vaao na lagaee, paarbraham sarnaaee. In paraphrase: the hot wind doesn't touch the one who is in the refuge of the Supreme Lord. Then the picture widens. All around me, on four sides, is the Lord's protective circle, so no pain touches me. I met the true Guru, who made this happen; he gave me the medicine of the Lord's Name. Three images hold it together. Taatee vaao, the hot wind, stands for whatever scorches: illness, fear, cruelty, grief. Sarnaaee is refuge, sanctuary, the place you run to. And the circle on four sides is a line drawn around you, a protected space, a boundary harm can't cross. Then the last image quietly answers a hard question. The Guru gives a medicine, aukhadh: the Name. Nobody hands medicine to someone who is perfectly well. So the shabad doesn't picture a life where nothing ever scorches. It pictures someone who has been given what heals, with a line drawn around them while the wind blows. It is sung in hospital rooms, before journeys, when a baby is born, or simply at night. It isn't a charm. It's shade and medicine, held out together.

segments.voice: Move, if you can, to the coolest, quietest spot near you, or simply close your eyes, and name one hot wind blowing in your life right now. Then picture a circle drawn around you on four sides, and rest inside it. If you pray, say Waheguru, or the shabad's opening words, taatee vaao na lagaee.

Your line: in his refuge. Shade and medicine, even while the wind still blows. Rest well.

668.title: Some say Ram, some Khuda
668.hook: some call Him Ram, some Khuda, some serve as Gusain, some as Allah (Ramkali M5, ang 885)
668.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this shabad of Guru Arjan in kirtan, and often turn to it at interfaith gatherings as a picture of neighbors who name God differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taatee vaao, the hot wind, and your line: in his refuge. Today, a shabad that walks through a whole street of neighbors.

Sunrise in an old Punjabi market town. From one direction, the call to prayer. From another, temple bells and someone chanting Ram. A man walks toward the river to bathe; another unrolls a mat to bow. Two neighbors greet each other in different words for the same morning. Guru Arjan lived in streets like that. And in one shabad he simply looked around and listed what he saw, without telling anyone they were wrong.
screen: `AN OLD MARKET TOWN AT SUNRISE.` → `BELLS, A CALL, A CHANT.` → `A SHABAD THAT LISTS WHAT IT SEES.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, on Ang eight eighty-five. It opens, in paraphrase: some say Ram, Ram; some say Khuda. Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Ram is a name Hindus use for God; Khuda is the Persian word Muslims in India used. Gusain, a Lord, a master, was used by Hindu devotees; Allah, the Arabic name, by Muslims. Then the refrain: He is the Cause of causes, the Generous One; He showers mercy, the Merciful. Kareem and Raheem, generous and merciful, are Arabic names of God used in Islam, sung here in a Sikh scripture. The shabad keeps going down the street. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads in prayer. Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books Muslims revere. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Hindu, some Muslim. Some ask for one paradise, some for another. It's a portrait of a neighborhood, drawn fairly. Then the last line turns. Nanak says, whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam, the divine order, knows the Master's secret. The shabad doesn't say the names are all the same thing, or that the practices don't matter. It says that behind every name there's one Lord, and what counts is recognizing His will. It's a shabad for living alongside people who pray differently. In its view, a neighbor's word for God names the same One.
screen: `RAM, KHUDA, GUSAIN, ALLAH.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM IN THE REFRAIN.` · `A WHOLE STREET, DRAWN FAIRLY.` · `RECOGNIZE THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES, ONE LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a name for God that isn't the one you grew up with, perhaps one a friend or neighbor uses, and say it silently once, with respect, the way you'd say a name you'd just learned. Then think of someone who prays with that name, and wish them well. If you pray, say Waheguru after it, and let the two names sit side by side.
Hukam, the divine order: Guru Arjan's shabad says some call the Lord Ram, some Khuda, some Gusain, some Allah, and the one who recognizes it knows His secret.
Your line: many names, one lord. A whole street of names, and one Master behind them. That's day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: Blessed is Ram Das
669.hook: the minstrels Satta and Balvand praise the Gurus' light passing on (Ramkali ki Var, ang 968)
669.tomorrow: I never knew what You did
669.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Satta and Balvand's var in kirtan, and quote its phrase about the same light and the same way when speaking of the ten Gurus as one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, the divine order behind every name, and your line: many names, one lord. Today, a song by two musicians about one light in many lamps.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and you find the Gurus' hymns, and the words of saints the Gurus gathered. But a few pages come from people who were in the room with the Gurus. Among them, tradition says, were two musicians of the Guru's court, Satta and Balvand, who played the rabab and sang. They watched the line of Gurus pass from one to the next, and they wrote about it the way musicians would: in a ballad, a var.
screen: `HYMNS BY GURUS AND SAINTS.` → `AND TWO MUSICIANS IN THE ROOM.` → `A BALLAD, A VAR.`

segments.voice: Their var sits in Raag Ramkali, on Angs nine sixty-six to nine sixty-eight. It's short, and it tells one story: Guru Nanak's light passing to Guru Angad, then to Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. The line everyone remembers comes early, in a stanza about Guru Angad. In paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the Master has only changed the body. Jot ohaa, jugat saae. That single phrase holds the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus: not ten different teachers, but one light passing from lamp to lamp. Then, on Ang nine sixty-eight, the stanza for the fourth Guru opens: dhan dhan Raam Daas gur. Blessed, blessed is Guru Ram Das; the One who made you has also adorned you. The same stanza names him as one with those before him: you are Nanak, you are Lehna, you are Amar Das. Why does it matter? Because the var is a witness. Not a theologian explaining succession, but two singers close enough to see it, saying: we watched the same light move. Sikhs still sing their var, and jot ohaa jugat saae is often quoted when people speak of the Gurus as one. And the musicians' own names, Satta and Balvand, are in the Guru Granth Sahib forever. The people who carried the tune are kept in the book.
screen: `TWO MINSTRELS, ONE BALLAD.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE WAY, A NEW BODY.` · `BLESSED, BLESSED IS RAM DAS.` · `WITNESSES, KEPT IN THE BOOK.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT PASSES ON.`

segments.voice: Think of a person you admire, and ask who taught them: a parent, a coach, a mentor, a grandmother, a book. Picture the light passing from that teacher to them, and maybe from them to you, and silently say: blessed is the one who taught them. If you pray, say Waheguru in thanks for that line of teachers.
Jot, light: the musicians Satta and Balvand's ballad about the fourth Guru says the jot is the same, the way is the same, and only the body changes.
Your line: the light passes on. One flame, many lamps. Six hundred sixty-nine days, and counting.

670.title: I never knew what You did
670.hook: I didn't recognize what You did; You made me worthy (Mundavani salok M5, ang 1429)
670.howItsDone: This salok of Guru Arjan is read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog, just before the Raagmala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jot, the one light passing from Guru to Guru, and your line: the light passes on. Today, a line about all the help we never noticed.

Years later, you find out. The neighbor who quietly paid a bill when your family was struggling. The teacher who argued for you in a meeting you never knew happened. The parent who skipped something they wanted so you could have what you needed. You lived through those years thinking you'd managed on your own. Then the curtain lifts, and you see the hands that were holding things up the whole time. A short salok near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib is about exactly that moment.
screen: `YEARS LATER, YOU FIND OUT.` → `HELP YOU NEVER SAW.` → `THE CURTAIN LIFTS.`

segments.voice: The salok is by Guru Arjan, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, right after the Mundavani, the seal he set on the Granth. Its first words are teraa keetaa jaato naahee. In paraphrase: I did not recognize what You did for me; You made me worthy. I am unworthy, with no virtue of my own, and You took pity on me. You had mercy, and I met the true Guru, my friend. Nanak says, if I receive the Name, I live, and my body and mind bloom. Look at the order. First, a confession: I didn't notice. Then the surprise: You made me worthy anyway. The word for worthy is jog. It sounds like yoga, but here it simply means fit, capable, deserving. The worthiness wasn't earned and then rewarded. It was given, and only seen afterward. Where the salok sits matters too. It's among the last words before the Raagmala, the index of raags at the very end. When a family or a gurdwara completes a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at a bhog, this salok is read near the close. So after more than fourteen hundred pages, the reading ends not with an achievement but with thanks: You did it, and I didn't even know. The same turn can come at the end of any long effort, a degree, a recovery, a hard year: you look back and see the help you missed.

segments.voice: Let your mind go back to one stretch of your life you think you got through alone, and look again: who drove, cooked, covered for you, prayed for you, paid for something? Let one face come, hold it, and say a silent thank you. If you pray, say Waheguru for the help you still haven't seen.

671.title: Tell the beloved friend
671.hook: the Tenth Guru's song in the wilderness after Chamkaur: tell the beloved friend the state of his disciples (Dasam, Khayal Patshahi 10)
671.howItsDone: Sikhs sing mitra piaare noo softly in kirtan, and it is often sung in December, during the weeks that recall Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the Guru's sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jog, worthiness given before it's seen, and your line: you made me worthy. Today, a song from the hardest night of the Tenth Guru's life.

A mud fortress at Chamkaur in Punjab, surrounded by a much larger army. Inside, Guru Gobind Singh and a small band of Sikhs. By the end of the fighting, his two elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, have fallen, along with many of his companions. At the Sikhs' insistence, the Guru leaves in the dark. Sikh tradition remembers him alone in the forest near Machhiwara, on the cold ground, his clothes torn. And there, it says, he sang.
screen: `A MUD FORTRESS AT CHAMKAUR.` → `TWO SONS FALLEN.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST, HE SINGS.`

segments.voice: The song is called a khayal, and it's in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings associated with the Tenth Guru. Much of that collection is in Braj, an old literary language of north India. This song is in Punjabi, simple and close. It begins: mitra piaare noo, haal mureedaan daa kahinaa. In paraphrase: go, tell the beloved Friend the state of His disciples. Without You, soft quilts are like sickness, and living in comfortable houses is like living with snakes. The water jug is like a spike, the cup like a dagger. And then: a straw mat with the Friend is better than grand houses that burn like a furnace. The Friend is God. A disciple, a mureed, sends word to the Beloved by any messenger who'll go. What's striking is what's not in it. No complaint about the enemy, no counting of losses, no call for revenge. A father who has just lost two sons speaks only of being apart from God, and of preferring the hardest ground with God to every comfort without Him. Historians debate when the khayal was written, and the tradition that places it at Machhiwara is just that, a tradition. But for Sikhs, that setting is how the song is heard. It's often sung slowly and softly: a tender song from a Guru whose life was full of steel. Grief, here, isn't hidden. It's sent, as a message, to the Friend.

segments.voice: Think of someone you haven't told how things really are with you, and picture what you'd say, plainly, without dressing it up. If you pray, tell God the same thing in your own words first, or say Waheguru and let that be the message.
Mitra piaare, beloved friend: Guru Gobind Singh's khayal, remembered as sung in the forest after Chamkaur, tells Him His disciples' state; the Friend's straw bed is better than any palace.
Your line: tell the friend. Grief doesn't have to be hidden; it can be sent. Until tomorrow.

672.title: Grant me this
672.hook: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai: grant that I never turn from good deeds and fear no foe (Dasam, Chandi Charitar)
672.howItsDone: Sikhs sing deh sivaa bar mohi ihai at gatherings, in schools and in kirtan, often standing, as a prayer for steadiness in doing good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitra piaare, the beloved Friend, and your line: tell the friend. It closes a week that held the hem, rested in His refuge, heard many names for one Lord, watched the light pass on, and gave thanks for unseen help. Today, a short request that Sikhs sing standing tall.
screen: `HOLDING THE HEM · IN HIS REFUGE · MANY NAMES · THE LIGHT PASSES ON · YOU MADE ME WORTHY · TELL THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: When people ask for something big, it's often comfort: let the test go well, let the scan be clear, let the money come through. Fair enough. This verse asks for something else: the strength not to quit doing what's right, even when it costs. Not to be spared trouble, but to stay good inside it. Sikhs hold it as the Tenth Guru's, and Sikh children learn to sing it.
screen: `ASKING FOR COMFORT.` → `THIS ONE ASKS FOR A SPINE.` → `A VERSE CHILDREN LEARN TO SING.`

segments.voice: The verse comes near the end of Chandi Charitar, a long poem in the Dasam Granth. Its first words: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai. In paraphrase: grant me this boon, that I never turn away from good deeds. That when I go to face the enemy, I'm not afraid, and I win with resolve. That I teach my own mind this lesson: to sing Your praises. And when my life's end comes, let me die fighting in the field. Start with the first ask: subh karman te kabhoon na taro. Never turn back from good deeds. That's the center of it. Courage in battle comes after it, and can be read as serving it. Then notice who's being taught: my own mind. The verse doesn't ask God to change other people. It asks for a mind that keeps choosing good. Who is Sivaa, the one being asked? Sikhs read it in different ways. Some hear Sivaa as a name for God's own power, the Timeless One, addressed by many names in the Dasam Granth. Others read it within the setting of the poem, which tells of the goddess Chandi's battles, and hear the verse as the poet's request at its close. Scholars discuss it, and the verse is loved either way. What stays is the shape of the request: a prayer for character, not circumstances. The Khalsa ideal of the saint-soldier lives in those four lines: gentle enough to sing God's praise, steady enough never to walk away from what's right.
screen: `DEH SIVAA: GRANT ME THIS.` · `NEVER TURN FROM GOOD DEEDS.` · `TEACH MY OWN MIND.` · `CHARACTER, NOT CIRCUMSTANCES.` · then, large: `NEVER TURN FROM GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit up straight and think of one good thing you've been meaning to do and keep putting off: a visit, an apology, a donation, standing up for someone. Picture the moment you'd want to back out, and picture yourself not backing out. If you pray, say the verse's first words, deh sivaa bar mohi ihai, or Waheguru.
Subh karman, good deeds: the Tenth Guru's verse asks, in paraphrase, that I never turn from them, never fear when I face the enemy, and teach my own mind to sing Your praise.
Your line: never turn from good. Not an easy road, but a steady spine. Day six hundred seventy-two, done.
